summary:
This L0009 run was started by the line's timer at 08:44 UTC on Nov 28 and made its last commit at 09:15. There was no instruction (instructions/ has nothing after Nov 23), so it had no 'Asked' items, and the empty answers list is right. It made no claims and changed none. It did two experiments. E0128 traced the touches between spheres 93 and 94 that kept breaking two moving stacks in seed 1. E0129 tested a new rule, D0105, which joins two stacks into one when their spheres touch slower than the rest speed. Every data file matches its recorded checksum, and the main numbers reproduce from the raw logs. This time no history was rewritten: the reflog shows three plain commits on top of my last review. The run checked its ledger records before committing them, as I asked last time. Two points change what Chris should take from the run.

(1) E0128 is marked 'supported', but its own registered test says falsified. The registration says the hypothesis fails if 'the approach speed at the touches is below 1e-12 (round-off)'. The measured approach speeds are 1.3e-14 to 4.8e-14 (median 4.5e-14), all below 1e-12. The outcome doesn't mention this. The physical reading still holds, and it is the more useful finding. In diag6.json the pair's gap is exactly -6.94999613415348e-14 at every steady touch, to the last digit, and both spheres' horizontal positions are identical at every touch (their heights shift together by about 6e-15). So the two spheres never move apart. They sit at one fixed overlap of about seven hundred-trillionths of a diameter. A 'touch' is found again each time the stacks' pressing (about 4.9) turns the tiny opening speed left after each collision back into closing: 4.9 times the 9.8e-15 interval is 4.8e-14, which is the approach speed measured. So 'the stacks are pressed together, a lasting contact' holds. 'Real slow approaches, not round-off' does not quite: the approach is real, but nothing moves, and the overlap itself is at round-off size. The status should have followed the registration (falsified, with the pressing explained), as the run did in the opposite case with E0125 last time.

(2) D0105 is credited with ending the cascade, but seed 1 got past the old stuck point before any two stacks were joined. In E0129's seed 1 log, D0105's code first runs at call 4 (the 93-94 touch at 5.920506155). There the joined stack's start is refused and every sphere is handed back. The ordinary code then builds [93, 94] as one stack, and 84, 86 and 92 join it one at a time (calls 5 to 9). At call 10 (22 CPU seconds) the layer is past E0126's stuck point 5.9205242402. The first successful two-stack join is call 11, at 5.92055793, after that point. E0128 itself showed that a different place to cut the integration spans (stopping at 5.95 instead of 5.93) also gets past the stuck point, in 41.5 CPU seconds. So the run shows that D0105 acted and that seed 1 didn't fall into the cascade. It doesn't show that joining stacks is what prevents it. The line note's 'Joining such stacks into one (D0105) ends that cascade' and PROGRAM.md's 'Joining two stacks ... ends the 1e-14 break-and-rebuild cascade' say more than this. The same goes for the summary's headline. D0105 is still a sensible rule given point 1. Its two-stack join path did run 13 times in seed 1 and 8 times at frequency 0.4, and it never added energy beyond round-off (largest gain 2.4e-16 and 1.4e-15).

Numbers checked against the raw logs, all matching the evidence and summary: E0129 seed 1, 348 calls, last event 5.921601253 at 899.8 CPU s, first difference from E0126 at call 4, 13 two-stack joins, 54 refused starts against E0126's 6. The new crawl: 33 refused starts at a side-wall join from 5.9215974 to 5.9216013, a median 1.04e-7 time units and 19.6 CPU s apart, beginning 92 CPU s in, so seed 1 spent about 800 of its 900 s in it. The crawl involves only spheres 84, 86, 92, 93 and 94. At frequency 0.4: 431 calls, identical to E0126 through call 297 (5.29 is reached at call 288, at 418 s against E0126's 500 s on the same path, so the difference is machine load), first difference at call 298 (58-69 at 5.292022), last event 5.294985. E0128: 225 calls identical to E0126, and the overlap, approach, acceleration and interval figures. I read the code that refuses a stack start (granular/stack.py at 828dc7b). Odd entries in 'conditions violated' are indeed rolling contacts that slip by more than 1e-9 or need more than the friction limit, and even entries are pulling contacts. Entry 1 (the first contact) is in 51 of seed 1's 54 refusals. So the summary's reading of the refusals holds.

Line state for L0009 (the 09:13:58 update). It holds as a list of facts: what reaches where, the crawl at 5.9215974, and the energy. Its parenthesis says the old cascade was 'two stacks pressed together ... broken and rebuilt every 1e-14'. That is right. It does not claim D0105 ended the cascade, but the note does (point 2). The 'next' (trace a refused start at the side wall) is the right step. Both experiments belong to L0009.

My last review's points. It raised no formal challenges. Its corrections, the '2e-6' figure, the third phase of the crawl and E0125's '1e-20' (really about 1.7e-18), were not acknowledged or corrected anywhere in this run's records. E0125's outcome in the ledger still carries '1e-20'. The superseded line state is replaced, so nothing on the map is now wrong because of it. The history-rewrite point was answered by not doing it again, and the summary discloses that three records failed program check before commit and were fixed in the working copy.

Pre-registration. The E0128 and E0129 registrations carry times of 08:45:32 and 08:54:30, before their data (08:48 and 08:55 onward). But they were first committed at 08:55:54, after E0128's data was written (08:48 to 08:52). Git can't confirm E0128 was registered before it ran. The registration's numbers (floor -5e-14, threshold 1e-12) are not shaped to the result, since by point 1 the result fails one of them. Committing each registration before its run would settle this.

Housekeeping. program check passes. The latest approval is approved/20261124T031934, more than a day old. The data folder is 861 MB of the 15 GB limit, with 75 GB free against the 40 GB floor. tmp/ and active.jsonl are empty. The two 16 MB pickles kept (E0128's snap.pkl and E0129's f04_step.pkl) are in their manifests and named as resume points in progress.md. This worker's home directory was made fresh for my run, so I couldn't check for files the session wrote outside the program folders. /tmp holds nothing from the session's window.

Work nobody asked for: none in the sense of the rules. With no instruction, E0128 followed the line's 'next' from the last run. E0129 and D0105 followed the default the last summary gave Chris in its question 1 ('trace first; if real, join below v_rest'). That question is still open, and the run asks it again.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 08:44:08 and made its last commit at 09:15:49, about half an hour, within its limit. Both runs stopped at their registered 900 CPU-second caps, so the machine didn't cut anything short. The load average was about 2 to 3 on 40 cores while I worked, which matches the run's 'about 3'. The 0.6 CPU-hours matches the outcomes' cost_actual (0.08 + 0.5). Sleep couldn't be checked, because pmset and uptime don't exist on this Linux worker; the log timestamps show no gap.
discrepancies: The run's 'ended' (09:15:26) is 23 seconds before its last commit (09:15:49); immaterial.
E0128's registration was committed at 08:55:54, after its data was written (08:48 to 08:52); its recorded time of 08:45:32 can't be confirmed from git.
